shows.title: to see love
shows.description:
Koji Tanada is known for carving single figures — often adolescent or androgynous bodies — from one block of wood, working with the grain and the tree's own irregularities rather than smoothing them away, so that the figure and the material seem to negotiate with each other in the finished piece. His sculptures have a quiet, watchful presence, standing or crouching with an interiority closer to icon-carving traditions than to naturalistic figuration.

"to see love" is Tanada's next show at Mizuma, opening in October; based on the gallery's checklist images, expect a small group of new carved figures continuing his practice of solitary, unfinished-looking wood bodies rendered with careful, restrained surface treatment. It's an opportunity to see recent work from an artist whose sculptures are held in Japanese public collections and shown internationally, presented in the intimate scale that suits his one-block, one-figure method.

venue.name: Mizuma Art Gallery
venue.about: Mizuma Art Gallery was founded in Tokyo in 1994 by executive director Mizuma Sueo. The gallery introduces Japanese and Asian artists with distinctive, style-independent sensibilities to the international art scene. As contemporary art markets in Asia expanded, Mizuma opened a Beijing space in 2008 and a Singapore gallery at Gillman Barracks in 2012, followed by an artist residence, Rumah Kijang Mizuma, in Yogyakarta in 2014 to foster exchange between Japanese and Indonesian artists. The gallery is known for active participation in major international fairs such as Art Basel Hong Kong and The Armory Show, and for producing artists who have gone on to international careers.

shows.title: Constellation
shows.description:
Takashi Makino is a filmmaker who builds dense, layered moving-image works by superimposing thousands of shots of light, texture, and everyday objects into abstract fields that feel closer to painting or noise music than to conventional cinema. Trained in cinematography and mentored in the London atelier of the Brothers Quay, he has spent two decades collaborating with musicians like Jim O'Rourke and Ryuichi Sakamoto, treating image and sound as inseparable materials.

Constellation continues the trajectory of his recent Anomaly exhibitions, which paired large-scale collage works on paper with immersive film and video installations exploring what Makino calls "anti-cosmos" — the disruption of settled order to reveal new patterns underneath. Expect a gallery transformed into a darkened, absorptive environment, with paper collages that function almost as storyboards for the moving-image pieces, all built from fragments of footage and paper recombined into dreamlike, constellation-like arrangements.

This is a return engagement for an artist who has become one of ANOMALY's signature names for pushing the boundary between visual art and experimental cinema, and it arrives just after the gallery's building-wide participation in Tennoz Contemporary during Tennoz Art Week, making early September through early October an unusually active stretch for the space.

venue.name: ANOMALY
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and National Holidays

shows.title: CHICKEN SAPIENS 2
shows.description:
Hiroki Kakinuma, a Tokyo-born painter who finished his MFA in oil painting at Musashino Art University, has built his practice around a recurring hybrid figure: a chicken-headed humanoid he calls "Chicken Sapiens," a creature that turns up again and again amid dense, panoramic scenes where the strange and the mundane collide. This show pairs new paintings of that world with the second run of a limited-edition resin figure made in close collaboration with the artist, following a first edition that sold out in 2025.

Kakinuma's paintings work a vein of surrealism that's more absurdist than menacing — his bird-human hybrids inhabit crowded, narrative-heavy compositions that read like stills from an invented mythology, equal parts satire and sincere strangeness. Bringing the sculpted figure into the same room as the paintings lets you see how a two-dimensional character gets translated into an object you can hold, with the artist overseeing the 3D interpretation down to the paint finish.

It's a compact but tightly conceived show: paintings, sculpture, and preparatory sketches for the figure all on view together, giving a fuller sense of how Kakinuma's private cast of characters keeps expanding across different media.

venue.name: Shukado Gallery
venue.about: Gallery Shukado is a Ginza art dealership founded in 2003 (as Art Office JC, renamed Shukado Co., Ltd. in 2006), now led by second-generation president Chiaki Tanaka. Based in a seventh-floor space in Ginza 6-chome, Tokyo, it deals in Japanese art from the Edo period to today, including nihonga and Western-style painting, calligraphy, rare books and ukiyo-e, alongside appraisal, cataloguing and export services. In 2016 it launched SHUKADO CONTEMPORARY to promote younger artists, and in 2022 opened GALLERY SCENA in Harajuku for contemporary art. The gallery exhibits regularly at fairs in Japan and abroad.

shows.title: Fresh Fossils
shows.description:
Waka Yoshida paints dinosaurs, mineral specimens and diagrammatic terrain the way a natural-history museum might, except every "specimen" is really a splice of memory — the plastic dinosaur toys of her Showa-era childhood, illustrations from decades-old encyclopedias, and the deep time of the creatures themselves all layered into a single image. Her paintings are often built around thick, box-like frames that read as display cases or wall niches, turning the picture plane itself into a kind of reliquary for preserving fragments of time.

This new body of work leans further into that idea of painting as preservation: pieces that treat memory as a physical, storable material, rendered with the same care a collector gives an actual fossil. The title plays on the paradox of a "living fossil" — a creature that is technically ancient but still moving through the present — which is exactly the tension Yoshida is after, collapsing the Triassic, a 1970s picture book, and her own present-day studio into one plane.

It's a tightly focused, single-artist follow-up to her earlier appearances at this gallery, and a good entry point for anyone curious about how contemporary Japanese painting is reworking natural-history imagery into something more personal and elegiac than illustrative.

venue.name: GALLERY MoMo Ryogoku
venue.about: GALLERY MoMo is a contemporary art gallery in Tokyo, established in 2003 in Roppongi. In 2008 it opened a larger space in Ryogoku, and in 2013 the original Roppongi space was reopened as GALLERY MoMo Projects, focused on discovering young Japanese and international artists and curators. The gallery mainly represents Japanese artists born in the 1970s and 1980s, whose work reflects contemporary states of mind through personal styles, while also seeking connections to a global artistic context. Its stated mission is to introduce international artists with distinctive concepts to Japanese audiences, and to bring Japanese artists to audiences abroad.

shows.title: here there now
shows.description:
TARO NASU opens its autumn season with a tightly wound group show built around the gallery's deep, decades-long relationships with conceptual and post-conceptual art. The checklist reads like a lineage of language- and system-based practice: Carl Andre, Robert Barry, Marcel Broodthaers, Stanley Brouwn, Ian Wilson and Lawrence Weiner sit alongside artists the gallery has represented more directly in Tokyo, including Ryan Gander, Liam Gillick and Pierre Huyghe, plus Philippe Parreno.

The title suggests a loose curatorial premise about presence and location — art that points at "here," "there," and "now" as unstable, contingent positions rather than fixed facts, a concern shared by many of the conceptualists on view, from Weiner's declarative text works to Brouwn's walked-distance pieces. Expect a spare, cerebral hang heavy on works on paper, small sculptural gestures and documentation rather than spectacle.

It's a rare chance in Tokyo to see this generation of European and American conceptualism in dialogue with the artists TARO NASU has championed since the 2000s, in a gallery that has quietly built one of the city's most historically literate contemporary programs.

venue.name: TARO NASU
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and national holidays

shows.title: Sign
shows.description:
Tetsuya Umeda works less like a sculptor than a stage director for physics: his installations are chain reactions of found objects, water, air pressure, light and sound that he assembles on site, letting materials trigger and interrupt one another in loops that are never quite fully controllable. For this Ota Fine Arts show, titled simply "Sign," he turns that improvisatory method toward the idea of the unintended signal — the notion that meaning can arrive unbidden, read into phenomena that were never addressed to anyone in particular.

Umeda has described wanting to stage something like an "unguided tour" through the gallery, and knowing his practice, that likely means visitors will encounter kinetic assemblages of everyday hardware — motors, buckets, tubing, light bulbs — that hum, drip, and flicker into brief, precarious compositions rather than sitting as static objects.

It's a chance to see one of Japan's most inventive installation artists work in a commercial gallery context, translating a practice built for biennials and site-specific commissions into the more intimate, contained footprint of the Roppongi space.

venue.name: Ota Fine Arts
venue.about: Ota Fine Arts was founded in 1994 in Tokyo, initially in the Ebisu area, and has long positioned itself as a pioneer of Japanese contemporary art, notably giving early support to Yayoi Kusama. The gallery moved to Roppongi in 2003, relocated to the Tokyo bay area, and returned to a renewed Roppongi space in 2011. It later opened a nearby viewing room, 7CHOME, near the National Art Center. The gallery expanded internationally with a Singapore space at Gillman Barracks in 2012 and a Shanghai gallery in 2017, which reopened in the Rockbund district in 2023. Ota Fine Arts represents artists working in painting, video, craft and installation, with a program emphasizing dialogue among East and Southeast Asian, and more recently Middle Eastern, artists.

shows.title: Points of Entry
shows.description:
Kour Pour's paintings borrow the visual grammar of Persian carpets, block-printed textiles, and other patterned decorative traditions, then rebuild them by hand in acrylic and block-printing ink on canvas — a labor-intensive process that treats motifs usually seen as background or craft as the whole subject of a picture. Los Angeles-born and of Iranian and British descent, Pour has spent his career working through what gets called "high" and "low" art, "Eastern" and "Western" design vocabularies, and how patterns migrate and mutate as they travel between cultures and centuries.

This is his solo exhibition at Kotaro Nukaga's Roppongi space, following the gallery's guest-curated summer program; based on the artist's recent series, expect dense, richly layered canvases in which repeated ornamental units build into larger fields, functioning simultaneously as abstract painting and as a kind of forensic reconstruction of textile history. Pour's work rewards close looking — motifs that read as pattern from a distance resolve into individually worked passages up close, evidence of the show's title: multiple points of entry into the same accumulated image.

shows.title: Points of Entry
shows.description:
Kour Pour's paintings borrow the visual grammar of Persian carpets, Japanese woodblock prints, and other decorative traditions from across trade routes, layering block-printed ink and hand-painted acrylic into surfaces that look woven, worn, and reprinted all at once. Born in London to an Iranian father and English mother and now based in Los Angeles, Pour treats pattern and ornament as a kind of archive, tracing how motifs migrate, get copied, and pick up new meanings as they travel between cultures.

This solo show, his latest with the gallery, arrives with few specifics released ahead of the opening, but the title alone signals a continued interest in points of contact and exchange — the ports, markets, and borders where objects and images cross over. Expect large acrylic-on-canvas works built from his signature layered printing and staining process, in the vein of the richly patterned, rug-like paintings that have become his signature.

Pour's work sits at an interesting angle to the gallery's current Vilanova show, which just closed two weeks before this one opens: both artists are, in their own ways, interrogating what happens to an image or object once it starts circulating far from its point of origin.

venue.name: Kotaro Nukaga
venue.about: KOTARO NUKAGA is a contemporary art gallery founded in Tokyo in 2018 by director Kotaro Nukaga, who also runs the historic NUKAGA GALLERY. The gallery operates three spaces in Tokyo—two in the Tennoz district (Tennoz and Three) and one in Roppongi—positioning itself at the intersection of Japanese and international contemporary practice. Its program favors avant-garde and cross-disciplinary work, drawing on history, science and technology to question established art-world discourse. The gallery represents a mix of emerging and established Japanese and overseas artists, supporting their development through exhibitions, artist liaison services and participation in international art fairs, while aiming to expand the boundaries of conventional gallery programming.
